946.title: Raja Yoga)
946.hook: nobody asks a chemistry student to take the textbook on faith: sooner or later, there's a lab
946.carry: the lab is the mind itself
946.howItsDone: Vivekananda's Raja Yoga is read and studied in Ramakrishna Mission and Vedanta Society centers, often alongside Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, and students describe starting with posture, breath and watching the mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a week of work ended with Karma Yoga's ideal: the silence of the desert in the middle of the busiest street.
screen: `KARMA YOGA.` · `A DESERT IN THE BUSY STREET.`

segments.voice: Nobody asks a chemistry student to take the textbook on faith. Sooner or later there's a lab, a pair of goggles, and a teacher saying, don't trust me, watch what happens. Vivekananda opened his book Raja Yoga with that kind of offer, made about the mind. Last week asked how you find the quiet in the middle of work. This book is his answer, and it starts by asking you not to believe him yet.
screen: `A TEXTBOOK, OR A LAB?` → `DON'T TRUST ME, WATCH.` → `A BOOK ABOUT THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Raja Yoga is his book on the yoga of the mind. Its second half carries his rendering of Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, the text this path met much earlier, the one that opens: now, the teaching of yoga. The first half is his own teaching, and it begins with an argument. The great teachers of religion, he says, did not only believe. They saw. They spoke of what they had perceived for themselves. And if one person has perceived something, he says, others can perceive it too, given the right method. So religion, in his telling, shouldn't rest only on someone else's report. It can be tested by experience, the way a science is. Raja Yoga offers a practical method for that testing, and it asks for no belief at the start. Try it, and see what you find. Then the twist. The lab isn't somewhere else. The instrument is the mind itself, and the first problem is that it doesn't hold still long enough to observe anything. So before any great experience, the book gets very practical: posture, breath, and above all, learning to watch and gather the mind. Karma Yoga said do your work and let go of what comes. Raja Yoga turns around and studies the one doing the work. Same teacher. A different door into the same house.
screen: `THE TEACHERS DIDN'T ONLY BELIEVE; THEY SAW.` · `WHAT ONE PERSON PERCEIVES, OTHERS CAN.` · `TEST IT, DON'T JUST BELIEVE IT.` · `THE LAB IS THE MIND ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Treat this sit as a first experiment: back upright but easy, the breath at its own pace, nothing to reach. Every few breaths, ask quietly what your mind is doing right now, planning, remembering, listening, drifting, answer honestly with one word, and go back to the breath. If you pray, you can begin or end with a prayer you already know.
Raja Yoga. Vivekananda's book on the yoga of the mind, which asks you to test before you believe.
Your line: the lab is the mind itself. Tomorrow, the experiment meets a monkey. That's day nine hundred forty-six.

947.title: Raja Yoga)
947.hook: a monkey, some wine, a scorpion, and the mind
947.howItsDone: Students of Vivekananda's Raja Yoga often begin with short daily sits in which they let the mind wander and simply observe it, before moving on to concentration practices; the book is read and studied in Ramakrishna Mission and Vedanta Society centers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raja Yoga, the book in which Vivekananda sets out a yoga of the mind. Your line: the lab is the mind itself.

Start with a monkey. Restless already, the way monkeys are, never on one branch for long. Now somebody gives it wine to drink, and it gets wilder. Then a scorpion stings it, and it leaps about in pain. And then, as if that weren't enough, a demon gets inside it. That's the creature Vivekananda asks his readers to look at in Raja Yoga. He isn't talking about animals. He's describing the thing doing the reading.
screen: `A RESTLESS MONKEY.` → `WINE, A SCORPION, A DEMON.` → `HE MEANS THE MIND.`

segments.voice: The picture comes in his chapter on pratyahara and dharana, drawing the mind in and holding it steady. He takes it piece by piece. The mind is restless by nature, like the monkey. Then desire gets into it: that is the wine. Jealousy at someone else's good fortune stings it: the scorpion. Last comes pride, the demon, and now it thinks nothing in the world matters but itself. You might expect a scolding next. Instead comes a gentle first lesson. Sit for a while, he says, and let the mind run on. Don't fight it. Just watch it. The mind is bubbling up all the time, like a monkey jumping about, and the job, for now, is only to see where it jumps. He's honest about what you may find. Some of the thoughts, he warns, may astonish you: you'll wonder how you could ever think them. Keep watching anyway. With practice, he says, the jumping slowly lessens, and the mind gets a little calmer each day. Watching comes first because before you can steady something, you have to know it's moving. Until the watching starts, the mind simply is the monkey, swinging from a worry to a text message to an old argument, and calling it thinking. The moment a jump is noticed, there's a little gap. The one watching and the jump are not quite the same thing anymore. That gap is where Raja Yoga begins.
screen: `THE MONKEY IS RESTLESS BY NATURE.` · `WINE, SCORPION, DEMON: DESIRE, JEALOUSY, PRIDE.` · `FIRST LESSON: LET IT RUN, AND WATCH.` · then, large: `NOTICE THE JUMP.`

segments.voice: Try the first lesson exactly as it's given: don't try to calm anything, let the mind run, and when a thought jumps up, a plan, a memory, a complaint, just notice it, the way you'd watch a monkey move between branches from a park bench. No chasing it, no shooing it away, and if a thought comes that you'd rather not have, let it be seen too. If you pray, you can hold the watching itself as your prayer.
Raja Yoga. Vivekananda's book on the yoga of the mind, and the path it describes, which begins by simply watching the mind jump.
Your line: watch the monkey jump. Tomorrow, another of his pictures: a lake, and what lives at the bottom of it. Day nine hundred forty-seven, and counting.

948.title: Raja Yoga)
948.hook: you can't see the bottom of a lake while the wind is blowing
948.howItsDone: People who follow Vivekananda's teaching read Patanjali's Yoga Sutras with his explanations and keep a daily sit aimed at quieting the mind; the Ramakrishna Mission and Vedanta Societies hold classes on the text.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raja Yoga's monkey: restless, drunk on desire, stung by jealousy, possessed by pride. The first lesson was simply to watch it jump.

Stand at the edge of a lake on a windy afternoon. The surface is all chop and glitter. Somewhere down there are stones, weeds, maybe a lost key, but you can't see any of it. Come back at dawn, when the air is still. The same water. Now you can count the pebbles. Nothing was added to the lake overnight. Something was taken away. Vivekananda uses that lake to explain one short line near the start of the Yoga Sutras.
screen: `A LAKE ON A WINDY DAY.` → `THE SAME LAKE AT DAWN.` → `NOTHING ADDED. SOMETHING STILLED.`

segments.voice: Raja Yoga carries, in its second half, Vivekananda's own rendering of the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, short lines with his explanation under each. Near the very start is the line that says what yoga is. Put plainly: yoga is the stilling of the waves of the mind. The Sanskrit word for the mind-stuff is chitta. The word for its waves, the shapes it keeps taking, is vritti. And Vivekananda reaches for a lake. The bottom of the lake, he says, is our own true self. The lake is the chitta, and the waves are the vrittis. While the surface is rippled, we can't see the bottom. If the water is muddy, we can't see it either. Only when the water is clear and the waves die down do we see what was there the whole time. That changes the goal. Nobody has to build a self, or earn one, or go and find one somewhere else. In this picture it's already lying at the bottom, and the work is to let the surface settle. So yesterday's monkey and today's lake belong together. Watching the monkey shows you where the wind is coming from. Stilling the waves is what the watching is for. Vivekananda doesn't pretend it's quick. The waves keep rising: a craving, an insult remembered, a plan for tomorrow. Each one hides the bottom for a while. Each time one settles, the water is a little clearer.
screen: `YOGA STILLS THE WAVES OF THE MIND.` · `THE LAKE IS CHITTA. THE WAVES ARE VRITTIS.` · `THE BOTTOM IS THE TRUE SELF.` · then, large: `LET THE WATER CLEAR.`

segments.voice: Picture a lake, any lake, under a little wind, and each time a thought rises, see it as a wave on that surface. Don't push the wave flat; let it be a wave and watch it pass back into the water, big ones and small ones, and between them, for a moment, the surface may go still. If you pray, you can rest in that stillness as your prayer.
Raja Yoga. Vivekananda's yoga of the mind, which he explains with a lake: still the waves, and the bottom, the true self, was there all along.
Your line: let the water clear. Nothing is added to the lake, only something stilled. See you tomorrow.

949.title: Ramana Maharshi (Who Am I?)
949.hook: a visitor asks a silent teacher the oldest question, and the answers come back in writing
949.howItsDone: People who follow Ramana's teaching practice self-inquiry, turning attention back to the sense of 'I' and asking 'who am I?'; Who Am I? is read and recited at his ashram at the foot of Arunachala in Tiruvannamalai and by readers around the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vivekananda's lake: still the waves, and the bottom shows. Your line: let the water clear. Today, a new teacher.

Who are you? Asked at a party, the answer comes easily: a name, a job, a town, somebody's daughter. Asked at three in the morning, it gets harder. In south India, at the foot of a holy hill called Arunachala, a visitor once put that question, and others, to a young teacher who, tradition says, hardly spoke in those years. So the answers came back written down. The little text that grew out of that exchange is called Who Am I?, and the teacher is known as Ramana Maharshi.
screen: `WHO ARE YOU?` → `A VISITOR AT ARUNACHALA.` → `ANSWERS WRITTEN, NOT SPOKEN.`

segments.voice: The text starts with something everyone can check. Every living being wants to be happy and not to suffer, it says, and everyone loves themselves above all. Happiness, Ramana says, is our real nature, and to find it we need to know ourselves. And the way to know yourself is to ask: who am I? The answer moves by taking things away. The body is not I. The senses that see and hear and touch are not I. The organs that move and speak are not I. The breath, the life-force moving through you, is not I. Even the mind, the thing that thinks, is not I. Each one gets set down, like taking off layers on a warm day. If I am none of these, what am I? What's left, the text says, is awareness, and that, Ramana says, is what I am. It sounds like a riddle, but it works more like a mirror. When you say my hand, my thoughts, my mood, someone is doing the owning. Ramana's question is aimed at that owner. He doesn't ask you to believe an answer. He asks you to look. The text even names the old road it walks: each thing set aside as not this, not this, the phrase the Upanishads use, put into a few plain pages.
screen: `EVERYONE WANTS TO BE HAPPY.` · `NOT THE BODY, NOT THE SENSES, NOT THE MIND.` · `WHAT REMAINS IS AWARENESS.` · then, large: `WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Notice the body's weight on the seat, then a sound in the room, then a thought passing, and say quietly to each: this is noticed. Now turn gently toward whatever is doing the noticing and ask once, without hurry, who am I, resting your attention there without reaching for words, the way you'd rest your eyes on a far horizon. If you pray, you can let that resting be your prayer.
Ramana Maharshi. The teacher of Arunachala whose short text Who Am I? sets down body, senses and mind, and asks what's left.
Your line: who's doing the owning. Tomorrow, how to ask it when the thoughts won't stop. Day nine hundred forty-nine.

950.title: Ramana Maharshi (Who Am I?)
950.hook: a stick that tends a fire until the fire takes the stick
950.howItsDone: In self-inquiry as Ramana taught it, people meet each passing thought with 'to whom did this come?' and turn back toward the sense of 'I', in sitting practice and through the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramana Maharshi's question, who am I?: body, senses, breath and mind set aside, and awareness left over.

At a cremation fire, someone tends the flames with a long stick, pushing the wood in, turning it so it burns through. It's a plain, sober job. And at the end, when everything has burned, the stick goes into the fire too. Ramana Maharshi takes that stick and puts it in the middle of Who Am I? It's his answer to a question the text raises plainly: what do you do with all these thoughts?
screen: `A STICK TENDS THE FIRE.` → `AT THE END, THE STICK BURNS TOO.` → `WHAT ABOUT ALL THESE THOUGHTS?`

segments.voice: His advice is short. When a thought comes up, don't follow it, and don't argue with it. Instead ask: to whom did this thought come? The answer arrives on its own: to me. Then ask: and who am I? That turns the mind back toward where it came from, he says, and the thought fades. Do it again with the next one, and the next. Each time, the question brings you home. Here's why it works, in his account. All the other thoughts hang on one thought: the thought I. Worries, plans, memories, all of them belong to someone. Follow the I back, and the rest has nothing to hang on. So the question does the job of the stick, turning the other thoughts into the fire. And at the end, Ramana says, it burns up too. Even the question doesn't stay. There's a second picture in the text. Somebody asks whether a seeker first needs to study and count all the tattvas, the categories philosophers say make up the world and the person. Ramana says no. If you want to throw out the garbage, you don't need to analyze it first. Just throw it out. That can sound blunt. It's also a relief. In his account, you don't have to map everything you are not before you ask who you are. You only have to ask.

If you pray, you can let this turning home be your prayer.
Ramana Maharshi. The teacher who said: when a thought comes, ask to whom it came, then ask who am I, and let the question burn up like the stick in the fire.
Your line: to whom did this come? Tomorrow, the helps Ramana allows along the way: the breath, a name of God, and an elephant. Day nine hundred fifty, done.

951.title: Ramana Maharshi (Who Am I?)
951.hook: a restless elephant, a chain, and the helps Ramana allows
951.howItsDone: Some who follow Ramana combine self-inquiry with chanting a divine name, meditating on a form of God, or watching the breath, using these to steady the mind before or alongside asking 'who am I?'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramana Maharshi's stick at the fire: when a thought comes, ask to whom it came, then ask who am I.

An elephant walking down a street swings its trunk from side to side. It grabs at a banana stall, a branch, the edge of someone's cart. Nothing malicious. A trunk just reaches. Now give that elephant a chain to hold in its trunk. It carries the chain, and the reaching stops. Ramana Maharshi uses that picture in Who Am I?, in the middle of a plain, practical answer about how to steady a mind that won't settle.
screen: `A TRUNK THAT GRABS AT EVERYTHING.` → `GIVE IT A CHAIN TO HOLD.` → `RAMANA WAS PRACTICAL.`

segments.voice: The question who am I? is the main road in the text. But when Ramana is asked about other practices, he doesn't wave them away. He gives each one a place. First, the breath. The mind and the breath, he says, come from the same source, so when the breath is controlled, the mind quiets too. But he adds a warning: that quiet lasts only as long as the breath is held still. When the breath moves again, the mind gets up and goes back to its old wandering. Breath control is a help, not the destination. Then japa, repeating a name of God, or resting the attention on a form of God. Here's where the elephant comes in. The mind, like that trunk, keeps reaching for one thing after another. Give it one thing to hold, a name, a form, and it steadies. A mind held steady on one thing, Ramana says, finds the inquiry easier. So those practices aren't rivals to the question. They quiet the trunk so the question can be asked. He isn't telling anyone their practice is wrong. A person who chants, a person who watches the breath, a person who asks who am I: each gets a place, with a plain note about what each one does and how long its help lasts.
screen: `THE MAIN ROAD: WHO AM I?` · `BREATH AND MIND SHARE ONE SOURCE.` · `A NAME OF GOD STEADIES THE MIND.` · then, large: `GIVE THE TRUNK A CHAIN.`

segments.voice: First give the trunk a chain: the breath going in and out at the nose, or, if you pray, a name of God from your own practice, repeated quietly, bringing the attention back each time it reaches for something else. When the mind feels a little steadier, let the chain go and ask once, softly: who am I? Rest wherever that question leaves you.
Ramana Maharshi. The teacher of who am I?, who also made room for the breath and the name of God as ways to steady a reaching mind.

952.title: Ramana Maharshi (Who Am I?)
952.hook: out of the sun, into the shade, and back out again
952.howItsDone: Readers of Who Am I? return to it as a daily text; at Ramana's ashram in Tiruvannamalai, visitors sit in silence in the hall where he lived and walk around the hill of Arunachala.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramana Maharshi's elephant: a reaching trunk, steadied by a chain to hold, a name or the breath.

Midday, a hot road, no wind. A traveler steps under a tree and the relief is instant. A few minutes later, something across the road catches the eye, and the traveler walks back out into the glare to get it. Then back to the shade. Then out again. Ramana Maharshi draws that scene in Who Am I?, near the end, and he uses it to answer the question the text opened with: where is happiness?
screen: `A HOT ROAD AT MIDDAY.` → `INTO THE SHADE, AND OUT AGAIN.` → `WHERE IS HAPPINESS?`

segments.voice: Remember how the text began: everyone wants to be happy. Here, Ramana says where that happiness is. Not in things. When we get something we wanted, we feel happy, and we credit the thing. But what really happened, in his account, is that the wanting stopped for a moment. The mind went quiet and turned back toward the self, and the happiness we felt was the self's own. Then the next want shows up, and we walk back into the sun. The one who knows this, he says, stays in the shade. Close by, a line for anyone who feels too far gone for any of this. Even someone who has done great wrong, Ramana says, shouldn't sit weeping, I'm a sinner, how can I be saved? Drop the thought I'm a sinner, he says, and get on with the inquiry. The heavy story about yourself is one more thought, and it gets the same question as the rest. Now look back at this week. Vivekananda's Raja Yoga: a lab where the mind is the instrument. A monkey, wild with wine and a sting, and the first lesson: watch it jump. A lake: still the waves and the bottom shows. Then Ramana. Who am I?, with body, senses and mind set aside. To whom did this thought come?, and the stick that burns at the end. An elephant given a chain. And today, the shade. Two teachers, and in both their accounts one claim underneath: what the seeker is looking for was there before the looking started.
screen: `HAPPINESS IS NOT IN THINGS.` · `THE WISE ONE STAYS IN THE SHADE.` · `DROP THE THOUGHT 'I'M A SINNER.'` · then, large: `THE WEEK: A MONKEY, A LAKE, A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Recall one small happiness from this week, a meal, a message, a moment of quiet, and notice how, just then, the wanting paused; see if you can find that pause again without the thing, and rest in the shade. When a want pulls you back into the sun, or a heavy thought about yourself arrives, ask whose it is. If you pray, you can let the resting be your prayer.
Ramana Maharshi. The teacher who said happiness isn't in things but in the self, and that the wise one stays in the shade.
Your line: stays in the shade. Tomorrow, a different kind of teacher: Aurobindo. Day nine hundred fifty-two, the end of a week.
